subject: Business
title: The Invention of Debt
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Invention of Debt usable.

hook.text: In ancient Sumer, farmers borrowed grain before planting season and repaid after harvest. Credit predates coins.

buildup.text: Debt is simply a promise to pay later. It allows transactions across time, not just space.

discovery.text: Sumerian clay tablets from 3500 BCE record debts — making them among the oldest written records in existence.

twist.text: Debt crises aren't modern. Ancient Mesopotamian kings regularly declared debt jubilees to prevent social collapse.

climax.text: David Graeber argued debt, not barter, was the original financial technology. We owed before we traded.

punchline.text: Before money existed, people ran on trust and IOUs.

quiz.question: What are among the oldest written records ever found?

details.summary: Debt emerged thousands of years before coins, with ancient Mesopotamian temples recording obligations on clay tablets around 3000 BCE. Anthropologist David Graeber argues that credit and debt, not barter, were the original basis of most economic transactions in human history.
details.whyItMatters: Debt preceded physical money by thousands of years, challenging the textbook narrative that barter came first. Understanding debt as foundational to human economies reframes how we think about money and financial obligations.
takeaways: Debt records on clay tablets predate coinage by over 2,000 years
Ancient Mesopotamian temples functioned as early credit institutions
Graeber argues credit was the original form of money, not barter

faq.question: How did debt work in ancient Mesopotamia without money?
faq.answer: Temple bureaucrats recorded obligations in standardized units of grain or silver on clay tablets. A farmer could borrow seed grain and owe the equivalent plus interest after harvest. These recorded debts could be transferred between parties, functioning like early financial instruments.

faq.question: Why does it matter whether debt or barter came first?
faq.answer: If credit came first, money was invented as a unit to measure debts rather than to replace barter. This reframes money as fundamentally a social relationship of obligation rather than a neutral medium of exchange, with important implications for how we design monetary systems.
